title: India Plans Sixfold Increase in Health Research Spending With Sweeping Draft Policy
excerpt: The Draft National Health Research Policy 2026 proposes raising public investment from 0.024% to 0.15% of GDP by 2047 and shifting focus from academic publications to real-world patient outcomes.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's Draft National Health Research Policy 2026 aims to increase health research spending sixfold by 2047.
  • Current health research funding is only 0.024% of GDP, far below high-income countries' average of 0.27%.
  • The policy shifts focus from academic publications to real-world patient outcomes through the ICMR-IRIS framework.
  • Priority research areas include cancer, diabetes, mental health, and AI-driven drug discovery.
  • The policy encourages state governments to enhance their health research investments and financing mechanisms.

  • India unveiled its Draft National Health Research Policy 2026 on July 13-15, the country's first comprehensive health research framework in 15 years.
  • Public spending on health research would rise from 0.024% of GDP to 0.072% by 2037 and 0.15% by 2047 — a more than sixfold increase.
  • The policy shifts evaluation from counting published papers to measuring real-world impact through a new system called ICMR-IRIS.
  • Priority areas include cancer, tuberculosis, diabetes, antimicrobial resistance, mental health, and AI-driven drug discovery.

India's Department of Health Research has released the Draft National Health Research Policy 2026, a sweeping proposal to overhaul how the country funds, governs, and evaluates medical research. Unveiled on July 13-15, the framework is India's first comprehensive health research policy since 2011 and is open for public comment until July 27.

At its core is a stark admission: India currently spends just 0.024% of GDP on health research, roughly one-tenth the average of high-income countries, which allocate about 0.27%. The draft proposes raising that to 0.072% by 2037 and 0.15% by 2047 — a more than sixfold increase that would still leave India below wealthy-nation averages.

From Papers Published to Lives Changed

The policy's most significant philosophical shift is how it defines research success. Previous frameworks largely measured output through the volume of academic publications. The new draft pivots toward real-world outcomes: whether research produces innovative therapies, affordable diagnostics, effective vaccines, or evidence that directly shapes healthcare delivery and government policy.

> **"India is the world's largest supplier of generic medicines, accounting for roughly 20% of global supply by volume."**

"India is the world's largest supplier of generic medicines, accounting for roughly 20% of global supply by volume."

A new performance evaluation framework called ICMR-IRIS will assess research based on its practical impact. Projects will be judged on whether they lead to new treatments, technologies, policy improvements, or measurable benefits for patients — not just journal citations.

Three-Tier Governance and Priority Diseases

The draft outlines a three-tier governance structure. A National Health Research Stewardship Committee will provide strategic direction at the top. The Department of Health Research will serve as the nodal implementing agency. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) will act as the scientific and technical lead, with plans for upgraded laboratories and stronger collaboration with state governments.

The policy identifies a focused list of priority research areas: cancer, tuberculosis, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, mental health disorders, maternal and child health, malnutrition, antimicrobial resistance, infectious diseases, and age-related illnesses. A dynamic National Health Research Agenda will update these priorities periodically based on India's shifting disease burden.

"The draft moves away from treating research as scattered projects and instead frames it as an integrated national system."

— Dose Daily News, summarizing the policy's approach

AI, Genomics, and Indigenous Innovation

New Evaluation Framework: ICMR-IRIS
›Focus on real-world outcomes, not just publications.
›Projects assessed on practical impacts like new treatments.
›Shifts from scattered projects to an integrated national system.

The framework places significant emphasis on emerging technologies. Artificial intelligence in drug discovery, genomics, digital health platforms, and national disease registries are all earmarked for expanded research. The government plans to encourage partnerships among startups, industry, medical colleges, and research institutions to accelerate the development of homegrown medicines, vaccines, medical devices, and diagnostic kits.

Existing Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories will be upgraded into broader Infectious Disease Research and Diagnostic Laboratories, enabling scientists to study bacterial, fungal, and parasitic infections alongside viruses.

What States Must Do

The draft doesn't place the entire burden on New Delhi. It calls on state governments to establish dedicated financing mechanisms for health research and gradually raise their own investments. Regular reviews of spending by both the Centre and states are proposed to keep the 2037 and 2047 targets on track.

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

For the global Indian diaspora, the policy has implications beyond India's borders. India is the world's largest supplier of generic medicines, accounting for roughly 20% of global supply by volume. A better-funded research ecosystem could accelerate the development of affordable biosimilars, gene therapies, and AI-designed drugs — products that Indian pharmaceutical companies increasingly export worldwide. The policy's emphasis on indigenous innovation aligns with the broader Viksit Bharat 2047 vision of a developed India that is a net producer, not just a consumer, of cutting-edge medical science.
